blocks.x: Today is March 22nd.
Today is March 22nd, yeah, 1986.
1986. It was an interview with Tommy Ridgely for the William R. Hogan Jazz Archive. All right, let me put my coat down and get my questions.
And I hope, and I say it again. We can all relax. Yeah.
Okay. Tommy, the first thing we want to start with, we want to get to this.
Okay, this is the second reel with Tommy Ridgely, send date March 21st 1986. March 22nd, huh? March 22nd on Saturday and we're at Tommy's house which is at 218 Arnold Avenue.
214 Arnold Avenue in River Ridge, Louisiana.
Okay, we got that out of the way. One thing I wanted to, when you were growing up, what did people call you? Tommy, Thomas?
Thomas. Thomas. Everybody know me as Thomas.
Grandmother, parents? Thomas, all of them call me Thomas. I didn't have a nickname. Your brothers call you Thomas? Yeah, they all call me Thomas.
And your friends? My friends call me Thomas too.
So when did Tommy come to you?

When I got in the music business and when I went to record, I went to Mr. Levy's office with Dave Bartholomew. And we sat down and I signed all these papers. You know, if I had a hit record I wouldn't have got no money I guess. Same way. But anyway, they discussed a professional name. And so he came up with, he said, well let's think of something. And one name always stick in my mind. He said, let's come with something like Memphis Slim or something. And I listened at him tossing names around and then I said, well look, I said, my name is Thomas Ridgely. I said, why not just call me Tommy Ridgely? That's it. And so this is what we sat on, Tommy Ridgely. Tommy Ridgely. But they talk about Memphis Slim and that.
Oh, you mean making it a professional name?
Making it a professional name. Yeah, yeah. A loose name that was talked about.
Yeah. Yeah, I was wondering. And I want you to, for the record, to spell Ridgely because I've seen it spelled a lot of different ways.

It's R-I-D-G-L-E-Y. Yeah, mm-hmm. Okay. Ridgely. That's, we're the only family around that spells it like that. Mm-hmm. Because I have had, I don't know, my daughter came and said, the teacher said it should be R-I-D-G-E-L-E-Y. Mm-hmm. But she said, no, we spelled it R-I-D-G-E-L-E-Y. Yeah.
When we're talking about family, did, was there a certain place where you, did your family eat together? Did everybody eat in one room or at the same time?

No, well, well, well, how that, well, we didn't have, we didn't have no, no eating place. Uh, I remember, I know as a kid we sat on the floor. Oh. My daddy, my daddy used to sit, and it's true, in the summertime he'd sit right on the top step in the house, right at the top step. See, we were living in the back. Uh-huh. And he'd sit on the top step. Uh, very seldom, you know, the table was, table had so many other things on it. They had no room to be eating on the table. They'd fix it. My mom fixed the food. Now, one thing I remember too, in fixing food, uh, the only person that had some meat was my daddy. Now, whatever he would leave, well, he would, you know, give us a piece of his meat. Uh-huh. Put that, my dad was the only one who had meat.
We had. What, what, what did you all eat usually?

Oh, well, um, I tell you what, we, we, we, we, we, you know, uh, typical red beans, uh, and I still love my red beans, you know. Uh, one thing, cabbage. My mama could make the best cabbage of her okra gumbo. Um, there's one thing my mama used to cook every Friday. We don't get too much of now. And that's fish cuvillon. And my mama could fix that. In fact, I don't hear too many people talk about cuvillon no more. How else it fixed?
How else it fixed?

It was, it was fish heads. And you get, my mama used to bring them back from, when she, my Sean on Friday, she'd bring these big fish heads back. Right. And she'd cook them down with a tomato gravy. And boy, it was good. Now, you don't hear talk, now that's another dish I like, but you don't hear talk of fish cuvillon. And this was every Friday at fish cuvillon. But it was greens, you know, uh, turnip, turnip, see turnips, smothered down in greens. And I still like spinach. Uh, on Sundays was when you had chicken. Right. See, chicken was specialty. That was, that was the dish, that was it. That was it. Sunday, yeah. Uh, and ice cream was a specialty. See, when, when you had enough money, you know, everybody had a freezer. I mean, the kind of ice cream freezer that you had to turn. And, uh, when you had that, that was a specialty. And they used to have penny parties. You see, they don't have, they don't have animals. What was, uh, a penny party? A penny party was, well, this is like for kids. Now, a penny party, you know, mama, you get a nickel or dime. Pardon my son. You get a nickel or dime on Sunday. And, uh, you go to a penny party, you can buy a penny, a penny with ice cream. And a penny for cake. And, uh, you know, you get a little, you get a little, enough for a penny. You know, you get a nice scoop of ice cream for a penny, and a penny piece of cake. And, uh, you know, a lot of people just like to have parties and things now. Well, they have penny parties for children on Sunday. And people selling it, I guess they make four, five, six dollars. And that was fantastic money. But that was a penny party.
Did, um, were there any special occasions where you would, where your mother would, did you ever buy you any special clothes for a special occasion? I had a pair of shoes.

If I had a pair of shoes, my shoes were strictly for Sunday to go to church in. I didn't even wear the shoes or otherwise. Otherwise I wore tennis shoes or nothing. If I had a pair of tennis. Like I said, the tennis I would go to school in, if I had good ones, and then when they'd break, well I'd tie them up a wire until we get enough money. And I do remember this, you know, tennis shoes was about 79 cents. Uh, maybe 98 cents. And, uh, and a, uh, suit, uh, good, had a pair of good for you. You know, you don't wear your good pants until on Sunday. You know, everything was Sunday. If there was anything good, wore Sunday going to church. Other than that, yeah. Put on whatever you could find. Cause I remember knocking the heels off old ladies shoes.
Oh yeah, winter time?

Well, you know, I knocked the heels off old ladies shoes and put two, three old socks on. You know, and this, you know, that's, uh uh. That's them talking, will that pick it up out there? Nah, nah. Okay.
Uh, I was wondering, was there any special meals on other holidays like Christmas and Thanksgiving?

Well. Or, uh, yeah, well, well now this is something, you know, I wish a lot of people could have seen. You see, down in Jefferson, Christmas Day. Uh huh. Christmas like was one big holiday. You go to, you go to, uh, you go to church Christmas morning. Uh huh. And then after that, it was one big holiday. You see how it was, they don't do it no more. We do it vaguely, but not as much as they used to. People used to get together in droves and come by your house. You'd have 20, 30 people at one time coming in your house. They'd come near your house and eat and drink and sing, a lot of singing and stuff. Leave that, go to the next house. And see, this was where our family was. And my aunt, my mom and sister, her name was Pauline. Pauline was a heck of a singer, boy. She sang, boy. And boy, you know, she would leave the singing and stuff. But we'd start making parties. This started going on by, say after people finished cooking, about noon. And it's going until 12 o'clock at night, Christmas night. But it's one, I wish, I wish things would go back like that because, uh, this was a Sue's Berry thing. I don't know if it was like that in town because I didn't go to town. But it was, it was a big party.
Did you, would you all sing Christmas carols? Uh, no, it was spiritual songs.

Strictly spiritual. You know, um, because like I said, you know the majority of the people back then were, were Christian people. See, it was more Christian, more Christianized and it was more real than it is now because I believe there's a lot of phonism with the thing now. But back then, it was real. You would, uh, you know, my aunt would sing, my uncle would sing, uh, and another man named Tom Sanders William, he would sing. And you see, there would just be one big singing thing. Drinking and singing and eating. He drank and singing. Not no, not no dancing. Oh, you see, you know, uh, if you went to a house where, if you went to a house where, uh, yeah. Yeah, yeah, we got, we got, we got the, the one.
Trying to be better than mine.

Yeah. But, but, but anyway, uh, this, this, this Christmas, yeah, the Christmas, uh, it was such a joy. Everybody would look forward to Christmas. You know, first thing, mom and dad didn't have money to buy anything. And so we'd go to two places. We'd go to Jack Sheen up on Central Avenue. He used to give away toys to all the poor black people. Poor people, period. White and black. White would go one day and we would go the next day. And then we'd go to Harmon Park. The Harmon Park, that was on, uh, Counting and Tulane. Right. We'd go there and get toys. You know, um, and then, you know, Christmas Day, well, that was a big day.
So you, do you, do you remember your parents ever giving you a present?
No, I, I can't remember because we had no money. Really. We had to go, we had to go beg something, you know.
We were talking about, you said, a lot of blacks and whites. The neighborhood you lived in up in Shrewsbury, was it all black?

Yeah, well, right, right, right, on Causeway all the way back, it was all black. Now, on, on, on, on, on Claybone Drive was white. We used to call it subdivision, that was white over there. But Causeway, and, and, and, and the, and the, the side street, all that was, all that, you know, like Andover Street. Well, well, that was black. Now, blacks were all the way over to Severn Avenue. And one street over, well, that was, um, what is it, man, man used to have a garden back there. Cause I remember when I was a kid, to earn money, we used to go pick okra, or pick beans, you know, and buy the hamper. And then, you know, I never was, I never was good at that. My brother, my brother, George, and he was younger than me, but he could pick some beans, pick some okra. I never did like that kind of way. That's why you, I tell ya, I went, I went, I went in my direction. Yeah, right.
Did you, do you remember a, a birthday party for yourself? Or do you remember?
No, I've never had a birthday party.
Not, not when you were, when you were a child?
No, never had a birthday party, no.
Or any for your, your brother's assistant?
No, none of us, no. Cause I said, oh, my birthday was so and so, that's it.
But was there any recognition from your parents that it was your birthday?
Yeah, oh yeah, we, we never let, you know, everybody knew about, you know, when the birthday was coming, but we just didn't have no money for no party. All the money had to be. No cakes?
No, no, no. A special cake or a special dinner or something?
Everything was for, to live. Ain't no money for nothing else.
Did y'all have any, since you're out in the rural areas, did y'all have any, did we grow any vegetables, have a garden, or did anybody?

Yeah, well, my grandfather, well, we didn't, I didn't have any, we didn't have any room to grow any vegetables, but my grandfather did plant, plant, in his yard there was a gentleman that had a big open field when we were living on Andover Street, right behind, he used to plant sweet potatoes. Cause I remember in the winter, we go, when he wasn't looking, we go out there and dig up some sweet potatoes and go home and wash them, and put them right in the ashes, in the, in the, in the, see cause of the fireplace, either the fireplace, which was buying the wood, or we used to go pick up coal on the, on the railroad, or the stove, just put the potatoes right down the mashes. And, uh, that's another meal. Yeah. Which I still say, you know, we ate sparingly, but I think the food was a little bit more healthier then. Yeah. Yeah. That's why I believe the older people today, the young people might get bigger, but I think we, maybe we'll, our body structure was a little different because I know from my body, but maybe I took care of myself. You know, I don't have to be no baron, but you know, I can say this, you know, I don't catch no cold. I don't get sick. And I'm 60 years old and I say, the good Lord been holding me for this hit record I got coming. I said, oh. Okay, we'll talk about that.

Yeah. We'll talk about that at the end. Okay. Okay, we'll save that for the end. Um, I was, uh, you said y'all didn't sit down at a table. No. Did, uh, but did your parents or your grandmother pass on any, like table manners, how to eat, I mean, you know, what?
No.
So they didn't tell you?

Uh-uh, yeah, you know, you don't learn this. You don't learn this. You know how to learn this, you see? How did, how did I learn? I learned by watching people. You know, like I said, because I did a lot of reading, uh, there were things that I learned. And, uh, oh, I gotta tell you about my school and see, we passed it.
We'll get to that. We're passing it out. We'll come back to you. But I wanted you to continue with where you, you said you did a lot of reading.

Oh yeah, well I would read, but, uh, I would watch people. Whenever I got in the company of people who I thought were on the other level, socially, I watched, I didn't say nothing, but I said that watch, because I felt like this is what I wanted to learn. Uh-huh. Because I always felt like, you know, I had to move from the status that I would in. What? And the status that I would in was down and down on the ground. And I just felt like I had to elevate myself. So, I watched everything that I thought would help me. And I would watch people. Anywhere I would go, and I can't name specific places, but any way I would go that, that I felt like, you know, things I learned, I'd watch. But when I went in the Navy, this was the turning point, really, in my life. And I was like, I'm not going to be a little bit of a thing. Because I think I, in going into service, now I, I joined the Navy the day I made seventeen. And, uh, I left here, went to Chicago, went to, went to, uh, Camp Robert Small. And, uh, I left there and went to Massachusetts. But I was always the eyes and ears open to learn. And I just, I learned things. I looked and, you know, I elevated myself. Uh-huh. You know, with, without the help, because I didn't have a formal teaching. So you, you felt a little inadequate.
Very much so.
And I had to learn.
And, you were poor. And I had to learn. Yeah, right.
From a very poor family, too. Very poor.
Okay. Yeah. Something about your, your mother, which I didn't, could you describe your mother?

My mama was the most beautiful woman in the world. I tell you know, uh, as far as for ways, everybody loved my mama. Uh-huh. You know, anytime anybody in the school, any little kids, any grownups, they wanted to talk to somebody, wanted her hungry, let's go see my back. That's what they call my back. Go see my back. Come in my house, the first thing she's doing, you come in and you know what she's saying? Right. I'm like, I want you.
Yeah.
To Johnny.
And, uh, as, as poor as y'all were.
As poor as y'all were, my mama cooked in a big pot.
Uh-huh.

And anybody come home can eat. Uh-huh. She always cooking, and she, you know, she can cook, and everybody knew my mama was a good cook, so she cooked good. I'm a little soul cooking. Right. And you see, my wife learned how to cook for my mama. Uh-huh. And, uh, my wife, she cooks. Yeah, I'm, I gotta invite you to my house and let you eat some, Ted, you think you, eat some gumbo, see some gumbo?
She got a single man. I go, I never pass a book. I mean, you know that.
Look, let me tell you about that gumbo. It's fantastic, wife.
So, was your mother somebody who was easy to talk to?

Very easy to talk to. And she's very Christian-like. Very Christian. She did not, you know, you know, the only, my, my, my, my, I've never heard my mama use a curse word in my life. Right. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. I saw, I've seen my daddy with a few drinks, dancing. I don't know if you remember the trucking. That was a dance.
Trucking, okay. Okay, I, ha! Oh, okay, all right. And you hold that finger. Okay, with the finger in the hand? Yeah, uh-huh. Okay.

And I've seen my daddy do the trucking, you know, I know, you know. But other than that, you know, he was kind of on a quiet side. But, you know, he'd get a drink. But my daddy did like to play cards, too. That's why he kept us hungry. Did he lose his money getting the gambling? My daddy worked, my daddy worked Monday to Friday. Get paid on Friday or Saturday, whatever it was. Come home. I used to, I remember this, he said, I'm in the door, shy his shoes.
Uh-huh.
Put on his clothes.
Right.
And we don't see him until Monday. Come back home broke.
Oh.
You see, but he was, but still he was a good man. But one thing, my daddy used to fight my mama.
Uh-huh.
And this was one vow that I made because I remember this. I said, I would never fight my wife.
Uh-huh.
And she said, we never. We fuss. We fuss like everybody. Raise my hand and here, no. Think this is our man don't have to do that. Okay.
Was your mother philosophical about life? Or your father? Did you pass on something?

Well, well, yeah. My, my, you know, my mama was only interested in us just being good people. That's all. My daddy didn't have nothing too much to say unless he, if he'd tell us to do something we didn't do it, he, and he'd get the strap behind us. Other than that, he didn't have too much to say. You know, typical. He, the mom, the woman was more or less the big thing in the house. Very typical.
So you, you, you saw your mother as the, the, the more authoritarian.

Right, right. Now my dad, then my dad, much more authoritarian because she was the one that set the pace, you know, what we had to do, you know. But one thing she's preaching, you know, be good people, you know, you don't go around stealing and you don't get no truck with them. And so that's why all of me, my brothers and sisters, you know, except that one, we got one, everybody had one in the family.
Which one?
Harold, that's Harold. He's, but everybody else, we're good, good, pretty good. We came from a pretty good family, you know, poor but good.
You're talking about getting the switch from the father. What, what, what, what, what would you have to do?

Well, well, I, I can remember one time my daddy whipping me. Because when I was small, we had a, we had a pig. Uh-huh. I just had to feed the pig. Now, we didn't have too many, what they call a slop in the hog. Right. When all the food that was left, we never did have too much left to slop the hog with. But anyway, what little we left, I forget to even give him that. One morning, my daddy came home, and I hadn't fed that pig, and he whipped me. And one time, I remember catching a whipping about not cleaning up the yard. Uh-huh. I remember I caught a whipping for not washing the dishes. Uh-huh. And my grandmother whipped me for that. But, see, see, like I said, what made us good people, we had, we had jobs to do at home. And you do them things.
Uh-huh.

And this is sad, I hadn't washed my dishes. I was on the corner, on Andover and Causeway with the fellas. My grandma came down there, and she was left-handed. I'm left-handed, too. And she had a willer switch. Wow. And she cut me right across the air. And you know what? See, when she got home, I was down on my knees scrubbing the kitchen floor. Yeah.
She gave me a few more lips. So, all the kids in the family had a chore to do.
We had something to do. Everybody had something to do.
Uh-huh.
And you know what? If you did, you get a whipping. It just made us better people, that's all.
So, of your father, your mother, which one played, say, a more important role in your life?
My mama played a more important role.
When you look, you know, in your neighborhood, who, do you remember who your neighbors were on either side and, like, across the street? Do you remember the name? I don't know.

Or the... Let me see. Going way back, when we were living back on Scott Street, Reverend Ivy was the neighbor on one side, I can remember. And there was this lady who was living with my uncle, and he recently died. I'm talking about my uncle Bill. That's my mama's brother. Uh-huh. And it was a lady he was living with. I can't remember who the lady was he was living with. But that was on Scott Street. Now, on... When we move up by my grandmother, next door to our house was the Owl Club, that big place on the Causeway. And on this side was the vessels. And all of the vessels are dead, and I except one lady. There was Miss Teenie, Mr. Mack, and there was the children, Laura, Laura Vessel and Mack Jr. And the house is going to have trailers. They have trailers there. And the Owl Club building is still there on Causeway. But, boy, no, that's going way back there, about 50-some years ago.
We all friendly with us, the people.

Yeah, very friendly. See, that's the only thing about how it was years ago. Everybody was friendly. See, I could walk out of my house and leave. We could walk out. I'd leave it open. I mean, leave everything open. Don't worry. And nobody steals nothing. You see, when I was coming up, there were the people that were bad or would do things were few people. And everybody knew who they was. And when something was done, those were people they would look for. And most times, 999 out of 10, that's who it was. So they didn't do too much, you know. Cause the people, everybody knew who the bad people were. But just in our community, everybody was still nothing. That's why it was so, the people that would go to jail, everybody would know about them. Because they were like one in a thousand. They were like one in ten.
You mentioned that somebody who lived next to you was living with a lady.
That was my uncle, Joseph Wilson.
How did people, how did the community feel about two people living together and were married back then?
Okay, I'm glad you asked me that. You know one thing?
How did they feel about that?

That was just part of, because that's been going on in the black families, period. That's the way it was. There wasn't too many marriages. You know, and if you trace black families back years, there wasn't too much marriage. There's more illegitimate children back then than there are today. Because that was the way of life. You know, people really don't say too much about it because it's a big thing today. But that's been going on in the black families. Well, been. It's been there.
So it was more socially accepted.
So it was, yeah.
I mean, everybody didn't talk about people.

Right. Somebody said, well, now, when a girl would get pregnant, everybody knew about it. You know, there wasn't too much to be said. Yeah. Because I know of one incident in Shrewsbury, I think, where, and it related to me, where this guy, I ain't calling him that, but he's married to his, what, first cousin.
Yeah.
Put it back as illegitimate.
Yeah.

And I see, being a small community, there was a lot of things going on, you know. Let me see, because my uncle, my uncle George Wilson, buddy, we call him buddy, was telling me about somebody close in the family wasn't married to somebody. Let's see, some kind of way, my grandmother, one of her brothers and sisters had another father, something like that. So, it was this been like that. Yeah.
Yeah, did, you talk about music in the neighborhood, and people visiting. Did people in those days sit down on their porches and play music?

What high it was, the houses that had pianos in them. See, most houses, any way people that had any kind of little money, they would all have a piano in the house. Mm-hmm. And, uh, my uncle, uh, Robert Wilson, he's a minister, he used to, he was one of these piano players like Professor Longhead. He played as well as Professor Longhead. Right. In fact, my uncle, my cousin, Joe Mitchell, he just died about, about, I'd say, two months ago. Now, this is his words. He'd say, ah, and that guy, he's talking about proper too, ah, that guy, ah, Toots. Toots Washington didn't want me around him, because he knew I could play piano better than
him.

That's the way he would say all the time, but he was a heck of a piano player. Boy, his fingers were that long. And boy, I remember when I was born, he used to whip that piano. And he'd say, Toots didn't never want him around, because he could play better piano than Toots. He'd say, and he'd say, he'd know that right now. He ain't gonna talk to me.
Sure did. What, his name was? Joe Mitchell. Joe Mitchell.
Joe Mitchell, yeah.
He played professionally?

He played professionally, and he went to, he left here and went to, he went to Chicago, and then he went to California. And then he, we talked about it not too long ago. He said, ah, I got hooked up with this woman, you know. And I, I started running on his ship, so he just, he was seaman. So he just eased out of the music business. But boy, he could play. And he always, he touched in one of them.
So he, he ran the same crowd that Toots ran one of them?
Yeah, yeah, he played, he played piano, you know, all the players that Toots played. And he said he was a better piano player than Toots was. Wow. He said, Toots know it. He said, you know it. Yeah.
So maybe we'll come back and talk about it. Yeah. Let's see, let's see more. I think we've talked about some of the things I've gotten.
Getting to.
Here, yeah. But, no, what I was thinking more of, of people like street cryers, people who sang. Did your mother sing while she was?

No. You know what, my mama was, yeah. My mama wasn't much of a singer. My aunt, Pauline was a singer. My aunt, Toot, her other sister. Aunt Toot was a, her name was Nancy. And Pauline and Uncle Buddy was a singer. But my mama was, you know, there was always one in the family that didn't sing to. Well, same way with my family. I have a brother. I have a brother. I have a brother. I have a brother. Not only can't, he can't sing, he can't dance. Louis, Louis can't sing and can't dance. Never could. But my mama, well, you know, there was always one in the family that didn't sing to. Well, same way with my family. I have a brother. I have a brother. Not only can't, he can't sing, he can't dance.
Louis, Louis can't sing and can't dance. Never could.

But my mama wasn't too much at singing. Well, you know, I heard her singing in church, but she wasn't a singer like Pauline and they took. Uncle Buddy and all of them. But everybody, everybody in my family, you know, had talent for singing. And in fact, the majority of them, it was talent for singing. And my Uncle Buddy, well, he's a minister now. He always said, man, he said, oh, I know I can sing. You know, he'd come and he'd let me hear him sometime. All right.
Well, as a child, we were talking about, like, games. When you were a kid, do you remember what games y'all played?

Oh, yeah, well, the games that we played, not the Spokin games, just the other games. Yeah. Oh, well, football. I played baseball, football. But I was never really good in basketball. But I was a pretty good baseball player. And I could run. I always could run by.
Did you play formally, like with a team?

No, we'd get out on the green. See, on the causeway there, right between, right at Andover Street, all the way back. See, we used to call that the green. They had a baseball diamond out there. And this is where all of our sporting events was. And they had a game out there. See, like this time of the OZ, they had a football game or baseball game all day. And you see, that's why I said that we came up the hard way. See, we played tackle with nothing on them. I mean, busting your head up. I used to go home every, I used to go home with all my legs bleeding, my hand bleeding. You know, from being tackled or tackling somebody.
We're pretty tough. Real tough. What other kind of games is a child, not sports?

Other than sports? Well, I remember playing hopscotch. We played hide and we played cowboys and Indians. That was a big thing, cowboys and Indians. You know, you got a dog, I got you. And hiding. And that's it. And then we got to, on Sundays, at the church, we used to go rent a bicycle. See, they had to play back on Metairie Road, where you go rent a bicycle for 10 cents an hour. And we go rent, I remember one. Yeah.
Was it tough for you to get to 10 cents?

Well, I'd find some kind of way to get it. Somebody, you know, shine shoes. Well, I kept a shoe shine box. And we go back there and run, sometimes, you know, sometimes I have enough to two hours. I'm saying 10 cents, but maybe it might have been Nicola hour. No, it had to be because they had different bicycles. They had the Nicola hour bike and they had the 10 cents hour bike. And so... When did you start shining shoes? What was the time?
Oh, I guess I was...
