Oh yeah, well, what I was talking about, the Black Carnival downtown on Arlene Street. You see, I mean, from Arlene and Claiborne on down to Arlene and St. Bernard, this was a Carnival, and then on Melford, I never did go on Melford Mean Street from, well, it's Martin Luther King now, from Claiborne on down to Dry. I never did go in that direction. I always went down and down. And from there, I walked Claiborne Street, and then I would go on Connell Street. But, you know, I wish some people had filmed that era of Carnival, and in a way you could see it. It was fantastic. It was really fantastic. It was something to see there. You know, a lot of things, Carnival now leave a lot to be desired. That's why Carnival's not as big with me as it gives me. You know how Carnival is big with me? How many gigs I can get. How many Carnival balls I can play. See, last year.
How was it last year?
I played 18.
Yeah, pretty good. That's good?

Yeah, pretty good. You know, 18. So from January 1 up at the Carnival I played 18 balls. And that's not counting the gigs in the middle. But I love it. You see, because I know, it used to be, although this year I didn't play, I played like Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, off Tuesday, and played Wednesday, no, off Tuesday, Wednesday, and played Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday. But I've seen the time where we had the whole thing. We played Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday. And that's where I won't get it back. It's tiresome. But the only thing you do is think about the little money.
You probably, I'm sure it's like most people, you're making hay while the sun shines. Right. The Mardi Gras.
You know what I'm talking about right now? You know how many gigs I've had since Mardi Gras? Two. Two.
Right now.

I've had two. That's all. And I'm off this weekend. I was off last week. I'm off. Well, we're going to play this thing next Sunday, my brother, for a dough. I'm probably going to make a quarter. But it really don't matter. But I'm doing this because he want to do it, not because I want. If I ever left up to me, I wouldn't play this. I feel like in my years in this business, I have already played that kind of stuff. So I paid my dues that way.
I noticed a bit over, in fact, since I've known you, that you don't do a lot of club days.

No. And you know, there really ain't no money. I don't know if you do anything. You work like him. Right. But you don't make no money. And I've just gotten out of that. I play. You see these people call me. I play with these people. I play for the Autocrat Circle. And from the time the band start, see, okay, I'll say this. See, there are Creole people downtown. It's more like white people. And I say like this. See, the reason we like playing for white people, people like me, is from the time the music start until it's in, they're dancing.
This is a little white.

This is the way the Creoles are. From the time the band starts telling, they're dancing. But you see them other black people, you know what they're doing. Sitting out looking at them. They ain't going to move until they get half drunk. And then when they get half drunk, then they want to start playing. And they can sit there an hour and a half getting drunk. And then when two o'clock comes, it's time to go home, they just begin to start playing another
number.
So there's a social difference. And then when you're playing, you know, you're playing a lot of people, you know, and I'll...
So this is a... But one question I had was, when is the first time you played for an all-white audience? When was that time?

When was the first time? Now, let me see, 19... It had to be 1956. And yet I was playing in a club. Well, I think I have... I can't remember, but I was playing in a club. I was playing at Jimmy Milano's, right where... Right at Dantino, where Jed used to be. Oh, okay. I played there about a year.
And it was...

It was a white club. The black people used to sit around the back on Dantese Street in the back end. And they used to hear us playing. I played there about a year. And then I left there. I left there, and this is when Jim Russell came in and heard me playing. And he recommended me to garden Natale. Out at Natale. And so I went out there, started playing a jam session with the gondoliers on Sundays. And that started expanding me as white. A white artist. And then along came Herald Records to record me. And that's when I meet my girl. And then I went from playing about 5% white to playing about 99% white. And listen, I played all of the white colleges. We played all colleges and stuff. You know.
Was there a conscious transition to playing for all white audiences?
No, I don't think... Not for me. Because what I can remember is being an entertainer, the first thing you look for is who will accept you as you. The white audience accepted me as me. That was it.
To the black audience?
It was always harder.
What?
You have to work hard for them. And that's even today.
How do you mean work hard?
In other words, you got to be at your maximum best at every setting. See, so what I'm saying is this. You come in and the blacks first have to wait until they get half drunk.
It's getting back to that saying.

Yes, to accept you. Whereas white, they hired me from me from the beginning. Blacks did the same thing. But they got to wait until they get drunk to get into it. Whites accept from the beginning. Boom.
Did you feel you were appreciated more by whites?

I'll tell you what. And you just ask. Start with the Neville brothers, Irma Thomas, Gene Knight, Oliver. And just ask them. They're going to tell you the same thing I'm saying. Hey, man, look. If there was a way. Well, I could. You know. Now, playing these social clubs is a different thing because you get set into playing a certain way. Okay. You know that people are going to come in there and sit down. You know the other people are going to sit down until they get half juice. And then they'll let loose. And we know that the Creoles are going to start letting loose just like white people write off. So, you know, this is understanding. And me being a band leader, these are the things that I know. So I know how to give my band to the audience. And see, one of the reasons why I get hired, too, is because they say that, Bartome, you know how to play for us. And what they mean is that I'll play a mix, a mixture of music. I play some old, some new, standards. I play cha-cha if you didn't have to. And stardust. And things like that. Whereas a lot of the young bands would come in and they'd get to playing that loud, blabber, blabber music right off. And it don't fit the situation. Don't know how to play a waltz. You see what it is? Now, I know how to play a ball. I haven't played but one strict ball. And that was for St. Mary's Academy. See, when I say a strict ball, they have a king and queen. And everything is done in St. Mary's. You know, like a ball. Okay. Well, the blacks' balls are just a bit different. They have the king and the queen. But it's a little more loose. And I know how to play it. I got it copped off and they hired me for this specific reason. You know? No, no. And that's how I keep working.
Because you don't work, you know, to black audiences, I'm saying, you were working to whites, did blacks ever tell you, you know, why don't you play for your own kind?

No. No, no, never, no. You never get that. The only thing, and I'm going to tell you the exact words that Irma said, she said, I wish some blacks would hire me. But they don't even call Irma. Now, she played for the Zulus. And they were highly dissatisfied with her.
For what reason?

They said she didn't reach them. And I got this direct from them. Now, the gentleman called me to play for the Zulus. And I can look out here and tell you what date. To play for the Zulus on the 27th of February this year. He wanted, and this is the Autocrat Circle.
Yeah.

He asked me, would I play their ball? He said, they were dissatisfied with the Neville brothers. Uh-huh. They want me. So, I said, well, you know, I played for the Autocrat Circle. I said, but, and I said, let me tell you, because this is a money thing now I'm thinking about. I said, if you call me any time, and we get together and sign a contract, and agree on the money, I said, sure I'll play. Whereas they give me time to tell the Autocrat Circle I have another engagement, but I'll only be going for one year. And it's money. I'll take it. So, I'm waiting for him to call me because he said, every year, I'm, every year I'm recommend to play for the Zulus ball. Every year. But every year they call me, and I'm, I've been playing for the Autocrat Circle now about eight years. And he said, but every way he called me, he said, so he called me, it was two weeks ago he called me. So, I told him, yeah, he said, well look, he said, the first of April, he said, I will get back to you. He said, I'm going to let you know. He said, but I think you'll get it. He said, if you accept it, I think you'll get it for me. And you see, this is what's happening with all of the, see like the Illinois, the young Illinois, I already played for the young Illinois. I don't play any ball, but I play everything else. And Mr. Houston plays all these things. But, they are not satisfied with Houston, because he is too uptight. And they say, what Mr. Houston, what he's playing, he's trying to play for young people. Whereas, I play for all the people. And Mr. Houston is trying to change this thing, play for the young people. And the people who, with the money in the pocket, who happen to be the older people, is getting dissatisfied with him. So they all want, everybody want me. I love it. Yes sir. We were talking about carnival music. What other music did you hear?
Did you hear any brass bands on a carnival day? Well yeah, well you know, what happened, you would always hear some, there'll always be some

little marching club with a brass band. And I'm talking about blacks. There was always a band coming along the street, somebody playing, you really don't know who they are. But there's always a, you would always hear marching band. Now, Herman Sherman, you remember Herman Sherman? No, he died. He died. But he was one of these that was always in somebody's marching band. Now I remember one year, and this was either 1950, it had to be 57, we played on a truck, my whole original Untouchable band, we played on a truck, one of these big trailer trucks, one of these clubs from down in St. Bernard. They hired my band to play. And they said we had the best truck that year. But because of the band, see what happened with the guitar, and it was the first time I had heard it, because I didn't know about that converter that a guitar could hook to the battery and get electricity for his amp.
Yeah.
And Justin Allen was the guitar one of the best rhythm and blues guitar players that, and boy, we just lit up Canal Street and Ramport Street that year. But it had to be 1957.
So you all played on the truck?
On the truck, yeah. As it moved? As it moved, right.
Which parade was this?
I can't remember. I know it came from, it came from the 9th Ward. It came from the 9th Ward.
It started in the 9th Ward?

Uh huh. Came up. Came up, yeah. To Canal Street? Yeah, came up to Canal Street, and went, and then we went back down, we went back down Ramport Street. But, and we played from about 10 o'clock to 5 o'clock that evening, but it was hard. We had some fun. And it didn't make no whole lot of money either. Never was a whole lot of money, but it was so much fun. And you know, that's part of recognition. You know, there was a white organization I used to play for, the Pink Elephants. I don't know if you ever heard of Pink Elephants. I don't know if you ever heard of Pink Elephants. No. I don't know. Okay. Mike Ginnard. He's a big man in the fire department, in the union, in the New Orleans Fire. But Mike was one of the members of the Pink Elephants. I used to play for them quite a bit. But that was one of the white clubs I played for. I played for the lucky 69ers. Oh, I got a whole guy. I see all of them talking about now. I got all of these books in here. Who I played for? You know, I got to have my books from 1957 up to right now. Everywhere I played. Who I played for. LSU, Ole Miss, Mississippi, Mississippi, Mississippi, Mississippi, Mississippi, Mississippi, Northeastern, Southwestern. I got all that right there. We'll talk about that. But specifically, did you ever go to any funerals or funerals? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You played singles?
Yeah. Do you know who the brass band was? Who was it?
I remember Earl Anderson was a trumpet player. I know Joe Tillman was a saxophone player. And that's all I can remember.
A bass drummer? Yeah, bass.
I can't remember who it was. I can't remember who that was. It had to be about seven, eight piece bands. But we played all day.
It was a parade. Yeah, in Lutton, Louisiana.
I'm sure it was.
I was going to ask you some questions, more questions about nightclubs, etc. What was the roughest nightclub in town, the roughest joint in town?

What was the worst? Yeah, where you had to keep your head right. What was the worst? Let me think. That's a good question, too. You know, back then, any club could be rough. But I know they had In Good Town. In Good Town it was pretty rough. But the roughest, I can't think of the roughest club. None of them were coming off the problem. But you see, I always say when I played, you know, it looked like I always, maybe I drew the better class of people. Other than the San Jacinto that had them big fights, some of the public dances used to have fights, too, like the labor union hall when it was out on Front Street. But I've seen, I've been, now, I remember one particular Sunday evening at the Robin Hood, they had a turnout fight in there. And this is when I was with this lady, and Marino was with Harriet, and Moran was with Gloria Bell. We were sitting in there, and all at once they started fighting. And every table and chair in the place was turned over, and the policeman was in there. They had two policemen, and there was people outnumbered the policemen, and the policemen were standing in the middle of the floor with their guns drawn, and people throwing bottles and things at them. They couldn't shoot because, you know, it was dark, and they didn't know. And how we got out, we went through a side door in the alley, just about like that, and all six of us went over the fence. We didn't know how them girls got over the fence there. They got out of that club, across that fence, and I used to wear a hat, and I went back the next day and got my hat. That Monday, because it was a Sunday, it was a Sunday evening. They used to have a thing on Sunday evening at the Robin Hood. And that's the last time I can remember, I think after that, the Robin Hood kind of went on. It's the way it went out, you know.
What year was this?
Hmm, this had to be in the 40s. It might have been around 1948. Had to be 48, about 48.
Well how did the club like the Robin Hood, how did it differ from the city Dewdrop or the Starlight or?

Well the Robin Hood, Paul Gaten was playing at the Robin Hood. See, so this was before Paul Gaten went on Canal Street. And Paul Gaten was very popular, Anna Laura was singing. Singing. And she was very popular, and you know, it just drew its people. Well back then, all the night clubs drew their people then. You see the Robin Hood would be full, and you go around down to Dewdrop, they was full. You know, Armstead's Bar, they had a club right there on Jackson Avenue, what, two blocks from Claiborne, you know, going towards downtown here. They had a club on that corner down there. They had, well back then people frequent night clubs much more than they did because you wasn't afraid to go places. You know, I could leave home from Jefferson, catch the bus and go to town, and have fun, and come home two, three o'clock in the morning hitchhiking or something, and not afraid. But you see, that was then, not now.
You think that's the reason people don't go out?

Well, yeah, definitely. I know this to be a fact, you know, because I know with me, there's certain places I would go and I park where I can hurry up and get back to my car without too much problem. And, and, and, and, and, and, and, and the places I go, I'll be watching and looking, you know, because I'm, this is just the way it is, this is a sign of the time and it's bad. You see, and it's bad for everybody because the people that have money in their pocket, that's why they have so many private places now. And I, like the Autocrat Club, as an example. Now do you know, Ted, you ought to go up there sometimes. You know, I've. I know, I mean I know the place.
I've been there years.

I've been there. Well first of all, let me tell you, you go in there, you're going to see a lot of people, you're going to say, oh, these white people are doing it here, but they're not white, they're black. See that's the way the Autocrat is. Now, one other thing, you see when I play for the Autocrat Circle, when I play for them, this is when the place be packed with a lot of white people. But you know what it is? It's the black people who have passed over. They come to the Autocrat Circle dance every year, packed.
And you see more blonde, blue-eyed blacks than you would ever shake the stick out.

But you know what, that's New Orleans. I'm not only New Orleans, we played in Covington. And I remember the people that we played for, I thought they were black. But when I saw them, you know, well then I left, I kind of looked closer and I saw they were black. And so I talked, and we playing ball in this place, crowded, with a whole bunch of these few black ones. So I called, and everybody in the band was wondering. I said, well I'm going to ask some of them. When she got close to the band, I said, well what kind of dancer? I said, this is a white dancer, black. And she said, oh this is black. I said, well look, all them white people are there. She said, but one white couple. And she said, see that couple out there? She said, it's the only white couple. Everybody else is black.
What did everybody was white just about?
Except the recognizable ones, you know, the real talk. Yeah. But that's Louisiana for you.
Yeah. Well, speaking of money, in those days when you had to, when you got paid, did you ever have to hide your money?
No.
No worry about that.

That's one thing you didn't have to worry about, because there wasn't nobody there to, you know, like, see, during those times, the few bad people, who were bad, everybody knew them. And everybody was watching them. So they usually didn't do things where everybody knew them. They would always go to strange places and do things. And so the straight, they just didn't, it just didn't happen. You know, at the Dew Drop, we always talk about this now. You see, we would, the band, all bands would come in from their job. Like I played LSU Baton Rouge from 8 to 12, well, 2 o'clock I'm in New Auburn. Right. We would go straight to the Dew Drop. Find a parking place on LaSalle Street, somewhere around in that era. The top full, the station wagon full, all equipment. Get on out and go on in the Dew Drop. Nobody steal nothing. You do that now. You'd not, or you wouldn't even find a car. But see, this is how much things have changed. And see, this is what got everybody so fearful of things. Man, the first thing I do is when I come in, I want to get my equipment home. When I knock on the first thing I think about, man, look, take my equipment home. Mm-hmm.

Did you always work with the club? Did you always work for a flat guarantee? Did you ever get a percentage of the tape? No, no percentage. The only time, you know, after I had hit records, records that would sell, and you would go out and play for, well, the booking agency would write a contract you would get.

Say, $5.50. $5.50. $5.50 was a good price for a recording office at that time. $5.50 and 50% over $1,100. See, so how they do, I make $5.50, the promoter would make $5.50, then we split the difference. Yeah. And I can remember Shell Booking Agency booking me in Shreveport, and that's the way the contract run. I think I made a few dollars over, yeah. Yeah. But you know what? This was white, not black, because this was on When I Meet My Girl. And you know, I was more popular up that way. You know what I was doing? Oh, I was popular. And you know how that started? We played, I played in Alexandria at the community center. And boy, we just packaged it out, white, and we broadcast on the radio. And I'll never forget this. I was playing in the head of Little White Girls right in front of the bandstand. And when I finished playing the bandstand, boy, them girls jump up on that bandstand, and they jammed me up in the corner. And the police had to come get me, because they had me in the corner, you know. And you know, autographs, secrets and things. But this had this white, prejudiced police who was trying to see if I was trying to make eyes at this little girl, was there, oh, because she came up and told me how much she loved my music, when I meet my girl and all this. And she was so happy that she was from New York, but she was going to school up there. She came up and, but you know, I have always been that when I play music, I go to play music, and not seek recreation. All my recreation camp after I knock off. When I'm on the bandstand, that's why I say that's why I had a, could always go back. I had a business to do was play music. Yeah. Not seek. And this is what I instilled in the band. I said, man, look, we are going to play music. I said, let's play music. Anything you want to do, do it after we off. No more, and this is what it was. That's why I got along with people everywhere. And it just was that maybe we showed that we were there for business. Now, I know some black musicians that's after white girls, strictly. And one band in particular, I didn't call that name, but they were strictly after. And they got popular in town, but they also had quite a few Indians in town. And I noticed because I heard something.
Did you always have to be, did you watch yourself, like if you were approached by a white girl?

No. No, it just, you see, it's always how you carried yourself. You know, I think this is what it was. Now, I'm going to call it the Danny White Cavaliers. They had this thing, you know, in fact they had this. I remember one time, a policeman threw some bullets on the bandstand.
Yeah.

But the Cavaliers, down at the, because when it was out on the shelf, right by the canal. Yeah. But, see, I never had nothing like that to happen with me. But they were so much into the white girls. And all of them, you know how they used to do? And then, on Mondays, they would put on, I guess you heard this before. Yeah. They would put on a white, overall, like a painter. Get a white hat, get a bucket, paint bucket, paint brush. And they go to the white girl house, they're just born there to paint the house.
You never heard that? You never heard that? I never heard that one.
That's the way it was. He's just, that's the easy one.
Just a painter, just a painter, just a painter, just a painter.
I had an incident happen with me, with Lee Allen.
Lee Allen had this white lady that he was messing around with.

And this is way back in the game. And he told me, he said, bring him on Two Row Street, right off of St. Claude. I brought Lee Allen on Two Row Street and got him on the first block off of St. Claude. Lee Allen got off the car and he's standing behind the tree. And he said he had to wait until the light clicked, click, click. And he stood there and waited and the light clicked. And Lee Allen left. Now he left his horn in my car. He told me I'm supposed to wait for him, see. He go in the house, he get on, run, go in the house. And so I'm driving around the block, half hour, hour, two hours. Lee ain't never came out, so I left. And I brought Lee Allen home to my house. And he told me he just did be daylight out of the house. He might like to call him.
Oh, somebody.
So what I'm saying is, this is the way it was. Yeah. But um.
So there was sort of a two-edged sword.
Yeah, yeah, right, two-edged sword. Now, uh. It could work. But it could be bad too, see, like it could have been bad for me. Suppose, what I'm doing, going around and around the block.
Right. Yeah, right, I understand.
But that's the way it was, and the people that were into that.
I'll ask you something about that. What is the, and don't take this literally, what was the attraction of black men to white women? And I don't just mean the physical, what?
Truthfully, I'll hear my conclusion could be one thing. Forbidden fruit.
You think it was?
Sure, that's all, you know, because it's just a human being. But I can't get to you, you can't get to me. And that's what it was. You find a way to get to each other because it's forbidden.
Is it possible, and someone mentioned this to me, it was, you raised your social status.

Well, yeah, I think in a sense, you know, because if this white lady wants you, well, you know, you just raise your social status. And the same way with a black woman, with a white man. You know, because the whites at that time, that was the ultimate. And you just raise your status. And although it was kept quiet, but now I say this much, the white men did it more than the black men. Much more. And all you got to do is go around and look at the people. Yeah. Touche. Show the truth. I know a good, this jockey friend of mine got a son in this town, he'll call his name. I'll be putting out probably business, but he have a son in this, he's a grown man now. I mean, he look like he spit him out. And the woman, the woman was black as my shoe. And boy, fine looking copper colored boy with curly curly hair all over his hair. I think he went to California. Fine boy. Fine looking young man. Boy, I'm writing this, write, you know, Cal Hill Project. And you know what? Me and him used to talk about it, see, because he used to come to Doudrop quite often. And I say, man, I say, you seen your son later? And he said, I don't tell me, how did you find out about that? I said, well, I know the lady, man. I mean, boy looks just like him. I look more like him than his children by his wife did. Well, you know, we don't have to mention anything. No, no, I wouldn't tell. I wouldn't tell.
He's not. He's not. He's not. Um. Can you find a wall? Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

We're on the last reel for today, number eight, from Tommy Ridgely. Where did we leave off, where were we talking about Creoles? Creoles, yeah. We were talking about the Creoles having their own caste system. Right, very much so. And blacks having to come through the back door. Back door. Even at the autocorrect.
Right, blacks were not allowed in the autocorrect.
When you played through the autocorrect club, did you have to go through the back door?

No, I never was. It was a little bit before. That was before my time. But it was very much in evidence because there just was no blacks in the club. And now, to show you how much things have changed, the president is a POA number one black dude. In color, I'm talking about he's black. Yeah. He's very much black. And, oh, they're the nicest people in the world. You know, of all the people in the world, man, I'm in love with my Creole friends downtown. And I think they know it. And they go out of their way to hire me, and I go out of my way to please.
Did you ever have to go through the back door at a white club? Do you remember having?

Oh, yeah. Yeah. Let me tell you what. This is not a back door incident, but I'm going to tell you about an incident. I was in, I was in Shreveport, Louisiana, and we was playing at the country club. We was playing at, and it wasn't cross-play, because I played all the country clubs in Shreveport. But anyway, Buddy Wade was the drummer. He had brought his car up there, and he went on ahead of me. And when he got to the club, it was about 13 steps up front, up the, you know, to go in the front door. And now they had a ramp where bands would go in the ramp right from where you parked, right onto the bandstand. But Buddy, William was one of these egotistical blacks. He won't go in the front door. Now the policemen tell him where to, you know, not tell him to go in the back, but this was the way into the bandstand. And Buddy gets mad about this. Now Mr. Abby Goldberg was, by booking agent, he booked me quite a bit, all up and down from Shreveport on back this way. So, when I get there, Buddy's standing up there, mad, he's, and the policeman's standing over there with his hand on his gun. He's like that. I said, but knowing Buddy, I said, Buddy, what done happened there? He was telling me about going through the back door. And so, I listened to him, so I went and asked the officer what was wrong. I said, well, you know, what is it? He said, well, and he was very nice to me. And I don't know why people are always nice to me, but anyway, he said, look, he said, that ramp, he said, that ramp, he said, that ramp goes straight to the bandstand. He said, and I was telling him, this is the way he's going, but he had to take his drums through that way, but he want to come through the front. And I told him he couldn't come through the front, go through the ramp. He said, and that was all.
So he construed that that was the back door.

Yeah, so, yeah, so I went there, I said, Buddy, look, I said, man, look, I have told you before, because I knew what kind of fellow was. I said, when you have problems, I said, don't you jump to conclusions, let me handle it. And, oh, he's doing something. I said, but you got the wrong concept, man, because the dumb man was only telling you, right? And we all unload our stuff right from that ramp. But he's still there winning his job. Oh, sure. Yeah, that's the way he was. I've never had, I can't remember having a problem. Now, you remember, what is his name, Sheck Snyder? Sheck Snyder. I'm trying to remember this. Yeah, he was, Sheck Snyder was the manager of the Auburn Twins. That's Sheck Snyder. We were playing in a club across the river. The Auburn Twins wasn't there, but Sheck Snyder used to follow me too quite a bit. Incidentally, last year, he called me from over, he lived in either Slidell or Covington. But he called. But anyway, this incident was, we were playing, and this was doing a civil rights thing. Yeah. And Sheck Snyder said, he said, you know, Tommy, he said, I ain't prejudiced. He said, but the only thing I could never, I'll never want to see is black and white getting married. And so I said, well, Sheck Snyder said, the way I feel about that, I said, that'd be up to them two people. We got nothing to do with it. It's how they feel. Right. And if they want to get married and go through whatever turmoil they have to go through in life, that's them. I said, and I failed all people. He said, well, that's the only thing I couldn't see. But there's one thing he failed to look at. He was going with the Auburn Twins' sister. Gee. But you know, like I said, he was just an individual, so it really didn't end. Can you check something on this tape for a second? Okay. Can you smell?
Okay. He just got warm next time. Yeah, that's probably him. Yeah. He just got warm. Uh.

But anyway, that was, that was Snek's style. That's my buddy. And now we still, we still wound up being pretty good friends, but he just had his concept of that particular incident. And I didn't think like that, you know, maybe he don't think like that no more.
Wow.
Yeah. Anyway, that.
We were talking about people dancing, dancing, dancing. Did you like playing for people dancing, or for people sitting down? Did you like it?
Well, if the club, if the club was in that kind of way where people sit down and listen, fine. But if it was a dancing club, I like them to dance. But if it was a sitting down audience, fine too.
Did you play differently for a sit down audience?

No, same way. I think for a sit down audience, you would have to be a little more projective. You'd have to project a little bit more. And then whereas for dancing people, you know, people would be more interested in dancing. So, it was just, you know, you didn't have to project as much. You know, you have to do your job, but you don't have to project as something to look at. Whereas with you, you know, people looking at you, sitting down, then you have to keep them interested in looking and listening. Whereas the dancing. Or a jazz festival. Yeah. Oh, a jazz festival. I love it. That's one, that's one, I look forward to playing a jazz festival every year. Because first of all, it's a, your audience will be people who come there to see you. Right. This is what I like, you know. And every year, I get people from all over the world, see. And I love it. I got my, I sent my contract back yesterday. Oh, yeah.

Oh, as a songwriter, you know, we were talking about, because you, you write, we haven't talked about that yet, but does, do, I always wondered about dance steps and what comes first. Does the dance step inspire the song or does the song inspire the dance? Or where does, where does the songwriter, and does dancing give you inspiration?

No, no, dances don't give me inspiration. You know, I was talking to a young man the other night. He said, he said, you know, he'd get inspired by a relationship he had with a young lady. And I said, well, well, I said, well, man, I said, if I had to get inspired like that, I'd never write anything. Because, I said, with me, I'm from the professional side, I'm just thinking in terms of trying to come up with something good professionally. You know, not from nothing. You know, they're just trying to think professionally, come up with something special. You know, not getting to that, like this song I just recorded. You know, it's okay to talk about that, not to me. Okay, yeah. Okay, well, I just, I wrote this song, the song I'm talking about, I call it a boogie train. And I am talking about, I'm talking about a specific, I'm talking about a train that's leaving New York, going to every major city where people have changed their dancing to, you know, to get on this boogie train. Yeah. And we have a perfect idea, and it's really working. I got a good groove, and when you listen to it, you're going to know what I'm talking about. The groove is really good.
Was there any of the songs that you wrote, like in the 50s, for Harold or Rick, that was some kind of dance concept?

No, no, none of these, you know, just trying to come up with a good song. I never, I tried to write one dance tune song, and I never recorded it. I never liked it in Norway. Yeah. But that might be the hit I have, because I don't like it.
Okay, we talked about, you mentioned the Blue Eagle. Blue Eagle. Okay. Was that a rougher club than say?

Yes, sir. When you say the Blue Eagle, you say it's a rough neighborhood, rough club, rough people, used to come into Blue Eagle. You would guarantee on a dance night at the Blue Eagle, guarantee a fight. It was like automatic. You know somebody was going to get their head bust or something. You know, it wasn't that much killing back then. But they would fight. Somebody might get, occasionally you would hear somebody would get shot or something like that. But it's very occasional. But, you know, like I always said, you know, when we were kids, somebody would get their head cut with a rock. But, and you know, this is the way it was. Somebody had a knife and would get cut. But it wasn't killing as much as it is today, I don't think. But the Blue Eagle was a bad, that was a tough neighborhood part. It was just for fighting now. You know, just people would fight. Who ran the Blue Eagle's club? The Mayor of Rampart Street. What his name was? The Mayor of Rampart Street. Oh, Reverend Brown. Brown. Trump and Brown. It was the Mayor of Rampart Street. He was the Mayor of Rampart Street. And he was the one who had all the things at the Blue Eagle. In fact, the last time I can remember Bobby Blue Bland, I mean not Bobby, but B.B. King playing a dance. We played on the same ticket with B.B. King at the Blue Eagle. And you know what? And at that time, B.B. King was working for $350. Him and the band. Him and the band. And he had about an eight piece band. And he was a nice dude then. Of course he was my size too. He was a little bit, he wasn't, B.B. King was my size, maybe a little smaller. Yeah. And he was nice then, but he had a good band. The band was good. Very good. And because I remember one time B.B. King even had some people out of Count Bass' band. But he played, we played at the Blue Eagle. It was a great band. He played at the Blue Eagle. It was a Sunday night dance. I'll never forget that. But B.B. King was just in a, like I said, he made just $350 and we didn't have that many people either. Sure didn't. Was Sunday night a good night for the kids? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Certain things. Well, most of your big shows would come to New Orleans. It would be a Sunday night. For blacks. Yes, sir. It was early. I don't know. But it would be early. You know, like 7 to 11, 6 to 10, something like that. I remember seeing Louis Jordan. Louis Jordan at the, oh, oh, on Conti Street. I saw Sam Cooke and Jackie Wilson at the Sam Club. Can you remember the name of the club on Conti? And Roman? Yeah. It was the arena, the Coliseum. Coliseum. Coliseum. The night before, the Saturday night with Jackie Wilson and Sam Cooke, they had had a fight in Houston. I don't know if you heard about that story. They had a fight in Houston about who was the star. See, Jackie Wilson had this thing about him being the star all the time. And Sam Cooke being a nice low song, but they had, they had Sam Cooke being the star and Jackie Wilson didn't like it. So they got in the, it was a riff in Houston. The next night was a Sunday night. They were here in New Orleans. And so Sam Cooke relinquished the star spot to Jackie Wilson. And he went on. Now the reason I remember that was David Thalibuio band, we played before them. Yeah. And when they brought Sam Cooke home, he literally tore the joint upside down. And when it was Jackie Wilson time, the people were still screaming for Sam Cooke. Sam Cooke. But Sam Cooke, of all of the singers that I know, Sam Cooke was the most dynamic as a performer. And he didn't do all this jumping up and down and laying down on the floor. He just sang. And them people loved him. Now there was one other singer in that category. Little Willie John. Heck of a singer. Didn't do all of this stuff. Little Willie John, little bitty fella. Boy, just get up there and sing and just kill them women. I remember at the Dewdrop, me, Willie John, Ray Charles. Oh, me, Willie John, Ray Charles. And they had somebody else. But they had one other big star. We had like a grand finale on the bandstand at the Dewdrop. And, oh, Bobby Bluebland. Bobby Bluebland was in that group. And we all had to do a chorus of two and kept on going. That was one of the high points in my life, too, as a singer. You know, it was like a finale. Everybody was singing. It was one song, but everybody had their little spot in it. And this was, I think this was a sad Sunday morning thing. See, because that's another thing about the Dewdrop. See, man, the Dewdrop, everybody ended up at the Dewdrop. And from there, the musicians, you know, especially Sunday morning, they wound up at the tree on the one-brewing. But everybody else, and this was during the time a lot of whites used to come to the Dewdrop. You know, um, well, you know, this, because this is where all the good entertainment was. And everybody else who was in the entertainment business, the world, when they finished, they would end up at the Dewdrop. They were fantastic.
Were there any problems with whites going to the Dewdrop?

No. The police was more problems than anybody else. Because they was the one that would try to keep people out. You know, Robert Mitchum came to the Dewdrop. No, I heard. Oh, yeah. Robert Mitchum came when he was in town. And he wound up at the Dewdrop. They tried to get him out. He told them they'd better go fly a kite. They had a priest. He used to come to the Dewdrop every Monday evening. You talking about that? He'd get drunk? Yeah. He would get him in his, him in the black lady. I don't know who the lady, I can't remember. But I do remember. I won't say enough. She's still here. But I heard the priest. The priest would pull off his collar. And they would sit at the bar and drink their scotch. And one Monday, even the policeman came back. He wanted to know who he was and what he was doing. And the priest told him he had no business asking him what he was doing. Because what he was doing there was none of his business. And I can't remember exactly what I do. I think the police let him alone. But the police was more, they were more of the problem than the people. The Dewdrop could have always been one of these clubs. But it was the police that kept the white people away. And I think it was more detrimental because if whites had came to the Dewdrop at that time, we'd have a better recognition all over the world. You know, the Dewdrop. And it already have a good recognition, but it would have been better. You know, so.
Were any of the whites arrested by the police? Do you remember?

Not to my knowledge. There probably were people who were arrested. But not to my knowledge. You know, but it was just that the police would harass them. Because they didn't have nothing to get after them about. But it just would harass them. And a lot of people just stayed away. You know, they knew they're good, because it was good entertainment. There was no doubt about it. And I say what you want. People, anybody, people would like to go where there's good entertainment, even to the people. And people would try to get the Dewdrop and the harassment. I guess a lot of policemen caught a lot of white people on their way to the Dewdrop and found a way to give them a ticket or something. You know, just to keep them away. Yeah.
What do you think Frank thought of all this? Frank Panion?

Well, Frank, he would never see. You would talk to Frank in private, I guess he would say something. But most likely he would probably a little bit too drunk to say too much anyway. Yeah. He kept his liquor. Frank Panion, I don't know if we ever told you about this, but Frank had a drink. Anyway, he had to stop for five minutes. He had, oh yeah, he was, well, he's been allowed. He had a bottle somewhere. He had all kind of bottles. He said, I'll talk to him in the jar. He reached and pulled his drop. Check it out. Put it back in. And this was any time of the day? Any time of the day, any time of the night. Any time of the night. Any time you're talking, get him a lift. And he was very shrewd. I think I mentioned the time he sent me and the Aspiders. We went to Alabama to play. And he asked me how much I wanted. Anyway, he got me the $250. So that was good money to go to, go to, go to, with that Mobile. And he had the Spiders. I don't know how much they were getting, but I think it was four in the group. But anyway, we went to, we played the gig. No, he told me to go to Tom Couch. In, well, out now, anyway, he told me to go to Tom Couch. And Tom Couch was going to, tell me what to do. So I went on Tom Couch and he told me, he said, look, when you get there, after you finish playing, he said, they're going to give you envelope, so you stop back here. Okay. They gave me envelope and it wasn't sealed. And I went there for $250. And so, since it wasn't sealed, I looked in and it was a check for $750. I took this check to Tom Couch. And I, he took that and then he gave me another one. So since that had happened, I won't see. So I found a way to open that envelope. He had $250. The check was $500. That's his check. And so when I get to the dude drop, Frank Pena gave me $250. So he had $250. Now, I don't know how much the Spiders got. They might have got. They might have had a different thing. Or they might have got their money, you know, different. But anyway, Frank made $250. Tom Couch made $250. And I made $250. It's not a business. No, well, yeah, it was business. They made a business, you know. And like I said, $250 at that time was plenty of money. Plenty of money. Sure, I paid my band $20 a man, and $20 per man was plenty of money. That was good. Yeah. And you know, and whatever. I will say, you know, things have been fairly decent for me. I always was able to make a dollar here and there. And never, never, like I said, never really get rich. But I always kept some beans in the pot. And I always used that phrase because Benny Spellman could say it so good, you know. I didn't get the man, keep the beans in the pot, man. And that's what it was all about. And that's what it was all about.
What are some more things about Frank?
He's a perfect guy. Frank was into his own thing, but I liked Frank. I got along. You know, I played at the Dew Drop at one stretch for two years. Straight Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Every Friday, Saturday, Sunday?
Every Friday, Saturday, Sunday. In fact,
Do you remember what the years that was?

1957, 56, it's the end of 56. 57 going into some parts of 58. Now what happened, what her name was, not, Faye Adams, Faye Adams was one of the ladies. And this other lady, she was recording on Herald. She's a very, she's a good looking lady, black boy. She's dark boy. She's pretty. And she was a perfect lady. She was working the show with us. And she said, man, I can't understand how you can get so much feeling into your singing, sitting down. And you know, well she admired me, and I admired her for her abilities. As a lady, I she was a great lady. She was coming to our show. You don't see her until it's time for her next show. I think she stayed there two weeks. But she was a perfect lady. I think it was Faye Adams. But she was on Herald.
Yeah, I think she did.

Yeah, and she didn't say that. That's what it was. But she was a perfect lady. She didn't drink, didn't smoke. She was strictly in the business to get to money. How would she say? She said, it's business with me, and that's the way I treat her. But I played behind her there. I can remember playing behind, what is his name? If you want to play a card, baby. Girl, don't you know you got to deal some time. Billy Wright? Billy Wright. Billy Wright. I played behind Billy Wright there. I played behind Little Richard there. Escarito. Oh, we played behind quite a few. And anybody else who was in town at that, you know, having a big show, well they would always wind up at the Dewdrop and I played behind them.
So at that point, would you say you had the house band? Yeah, the house band and the Dewdrop.
The house band? In fact, when I went in the Dewdrop, the Dewdrop had went down. And when I left the Dewdrop, it was at a peak.
How do you mean it had gone down?

Well, you know, attendance was why people had started going to other places. Because, you know, bad bands always run people. And so after I started playing there, the place came back up. And I stayed there so long. But I said that's why I got to know Frank Fairley well, you know, know where he was coming from. Oh, Chris Kenner. I had an incident with Chris Kenner there. And when Chris Kenner had Sick and Tired, and I had rehearsed Sick and Tired for me, Chris Kenner did it in B-flat and I was doing it in Key of C. And so Frank Pena called Chris up. So I called Chris up to do a tune. And so naturally he wanted to sing his hit record. And I asked him what key. He said he didn't know. And I didn't think. So I played where we played. And it was too high for Chris. And so boy, Chris Kenner was a big Chris Kenner about that wide. Chris Kenner wanted to punch me in the mouth.

You don't get me on all that bad. You don't get me on all that bad. You don't get me on all that bad. Embarrass me. Oh, she cursed words and I didn't say nothing to him. You know, cause the only thing I said, well, he didn't know what key he was singing in. I played it. We played in different keys.

But we finally found his key. But we finally found his key. See? And by the way, dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear I must say, it must have been hard. Yeah, yeah.
I know, I know.

But here's what happened after that. After Christian went up to the top, come back down, I was the first man he asked for fifty cents to get him a plate of red beans and a dew drop. I didn't give him fifty cents, I gave him a dollar. I gave him a dollar and something to him, get him some red beans and get him a beer. Same way with Cato, you know. Cato, Ernie Cato was this fella, this is an almighty high dude. And when he went down, he went up and you know he came down too. But see, they all passed me, went up, left me where I was. When they came back down, I was still where I was. They had to always come to me for help. And you know, I was always nice to do that. And that's why I said with my good lady friend, you know, she's up there now. And I hope she has sense enough to be able to stay and treat people right because anything that goes up is going to come down. And she will come back down. And I hope she takes care of, you know, a lot of people and have all her business in order when she comes back down because she do have the wrong man in front of her, I think. I think he's wrong. And she's wrong. Although she said nothing really didn't happen until she got with him. But I think it was destined for it to happen for her. And it just so happened she met him. But I don't like him. I don't necessarily like him. He's different. He ain't my cup of tea. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. a lot of them big names that came in town, not only in New Orleans, but all the surrounding area. So you could hold the hill with book things, Senator Frank, Frank would book things, Senator Tom Couch, you know, so it was like around, and Frank had a nightclub plus a hotel. So the entertainer would come in town and play for him, and they would most likely stay in this hotel for nothing. So people had the chance to follow. As an example, Jan Brown came in town before he got big, he stayed at the Dew Drop about three or four weeks stranded. And you know, this is how people got to know Jan Brown, because he came out here with the Four Flames, see, Jan Brown and the Four Flames, before the band, it was a quartet, and he got stranded down here. Chuck Willis, Chuck Willis came by, he stayed at the Dew Drop, and he left the saxophone player, and he had never went back to Cincinnati. Nose, Nose was working at Wehrlein. Nose never did go back to Rufus Gore. Rufus Gore, never did go back to Cincinnati, where he was from, stayed here in North. And I remember the weekend when Chuck Willis was here, and that Monday I was going to Baton Rouge to play at the Purple Circle for Frank Pena, and he told me, take that saxophone player, he can play good. And I brought, that's how I met Nose. The first Monday night he stayed, he went to Baton Rouge with us. And that's when I got to know what kind of fella he was. Yeah, Trevor, yeah.
Is that why they called you Nose?
No. Yeah, it was. Well, other things I can't talk about on.
No, but was it?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
He had Nose problems?

Yeah. No, no, not necessarily no problems. I mean, he was doing drugs? Uh-uh. Okay. That's why I always thought it was Nose, because he did drugs. No, uh-uh, no. The cocaine? No, he had a big nose, but it was other things.
Oh, okay.

Yeah, we can't get into that. I just assumed it was drug problems. No, it wasn't drug problems. No, it wasn't drug problems. He was a nice gentleman. He would drink a little bit, but there was no drugs. And he could play, boy. He could play.
Yeah, I heard some of his records on King, and I assumed he was from New Orleans and then recorded, but he came down here.

He came down here and stayed. He stayed, okay. And boy, he could play. And you know what? He got to play, well, he just put his horn up and he was repairing saxophones at Wehrlein. That's where he was when he died. He just put it up and every so often I'd run into him, and he'd talk a lot of crazy talk, you know. But he's a nice fella, but he had his own way of life. That's what I say. He had his own way of life. So.

Okay, well, let's, um, I don't know if we could just stop there. I had, for now, um, there was something about the Dendler, a short question on the Doudrop back here. When you had a singer, a new singer came into town that you had to back up, would there, would you have a rehearsal with her?

Yeah, well, either we'd have a rehearsal or we knew that particular singer's songs that they would do. We would get a list of the songs that they would do, or they hit record, they had a hit record, we learned a hit record, and just go from there. You know, because for some reason the music was a little bit easier then than it is now. The music is a little more complicated because of the new chord progression that they use today. And, uh, back then, you know, it was more or less a three chord thing, or either circle of sixes, or either a two chord thing. Like with Joe, like as an example with Joe Turner. Joe Turner would just, find his key, and you know where he was, and you know what it was. So this is the way it was. You could find whatever song it was, it was a hit record, well, the band naturally wouldn't know that song. See, because the record market wasn't loaded like it is today, like they have a thousand hit records. See, because that's the way it is today. A thousand hit wearers back then, there was only a top ten or whatever, you know, and the most likely the band knew it. So it was much easier, much easier. And the people that you had to work with was a little bit more easier to work with too.
You mentioned Little Richard. What was Little Richard like?

Oh, man, you know, nicest man in the world. I mean, see, Little Richard and I were fairly good friends. He asked me to go on the road with him. He said, I don't want you to quit your band, you can go on the road with me. I said, man, I'm going to quit my band and go on the road with you. You know, same way Lord Price in so many senses gave me that offer. And you know, I always have been just a bit independent. I like to be on my own. I don't never really like to ask. When you see me asking for something, I've got to rush to end. I'm at the end of it. Then I'll go to the people. And when I ask you for something, I don't. I want to ask for something. Thank you.

segments.title: Opening of the interview
segments.summary: Date and archive are stated and the interviewer gets ready.

segments.title: Second reel and Ridgley's address
segments.summary: Reel two is announced and the location, Ridgley's home in River Ridge, is given.

segments.title: What he was called as a child and how Tommy Ridgley became his name
segments.summary: Family called him Thomas; the professional name Tommy Ridgley was chosen in Mr. Levy's office with Dave Bartholomew, and he spells out Ridgley.

segments.title: Family meals: red beans, fish cuvillon and Sunday chicken
segments.summary: Describes how the family ate, with no table, his father getting the meat, Friday fish heads, and penny parties.

segments.title: Shoes and clothes only for Sunday
segments.summary: Shoes were kept for church; otherwise tennis shoes patched with wire, and old clothes.

segments.title: Christmas in Jefferson, spirituals and free toys
segments.summary: Christmas meant visiting houses, singing spirituals and eating, with toys from charity giveaways because his parents had no money.

segments.title: The black neighborhood in Shrewsbury and picking vegetables for pay
segments.summary: Which streets were black and white, and earning money picking okra and beans.

segments.title: Never having a birthday party
segments.summary: No party or cake because all money went to living.

segments.title: Grandfather's sweet potatoes and healthier food
segments.summary: Digging sweet potatoes and baking them in ashes; thinks the old diet was healthier; hints at a coming hit record.

segments.title: Learning manners by watching, and the Navy as turning point
segments.summary: With no formal teaching he learned by watching others; joining the Navy at seventeen changed him.

segments.title: His mother
segments.summary: Describes his mother as beautiful, Christian and always cooking in a big pot for anyone who came.

segments.title: His father: cards, drink and fighting
segments.summary: His father danced the trucking, gambled away his pay and fought his mother, a vow Ridgley did not repeat.

segments.title: Parental discipline, chores and whippings
segments.summary: His mother set the rules, his father used the strap; stories of whippings for chores, and his mother was the bigger influence.

segments.title: Neighbors and a friendly community
segments.summary: Neighbors on Scott Street and by the Owl Club, and how open and safe the community was.

segments.title: Unmarried couples and community attitudes
segments.summary: Uncle Joseph Wilson living with a woman leads to remarks on how unmarried couples and illegitimacy were accepted in black families.

segments.title: Pianos in the house and cousin Joe Mitchell versus Toots Washington
segments.summary: Houses had pianos; uncle Robert Wilson played, and cousin Joe Mitchell claimed to outplay Toots Washington before going to sea.

segments.title: Singers in the family
segments.summary: Aunts Pauline and Nancy and Uncle Buddy sang; his mother and brother Louis did not.

segments.title: Childhood games, sports and renting bicycles
segments.summary: Baseball and tackle football on the green, hopscotch, cowboys and Indians, and shining shoes for bicycle money.

segments.title: Shining shoes for Miss Josie at the riding academy
segments.summary: He started shining shoes at eight or nine; the story ends with Miss Josie's boots at Carrier's Riding Academy after a reel change.

segments.title: Reel four begins
segments.summary: The new reel is announced and the talk returns to the Navy.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Boot training at Great Lakes
segments.summary: A country boy arrives in Chicago in a zoot suit without an overcoat; punishments in boot training and liberty in Boston.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Ammunition depot in Massachusetts
segments.summary: After leave they made shells at a depot for about eighteen months; he was seaman first class.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Logistics support company and the white company sent first to Okinawa
segments.summary: His all-black unit trained three months but a white company with less training was sent first and nearly wiped out.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Combat and skirmishes on Okinawa
segments.summary: Protecting supplies from the Japanese, shooting at people, and turning back from a sniper hunt on Sugar Hill.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: End of the war and discharge in December 1945
segments.summary: Eleven months on Okinawa, the false and real surrender, discharge on the lakefront, and meeting Emerette on the way home.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: What the Navy did for him
segments.summary: He credits service with teaching him to take orders and grow as a person.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Family and whites; touring the South in the civil rights era
segments.summary: His family had no trouble with whites; on tour he was treated well, with stories of Mississippi and a dance hall where bands played each song twice.

segments.chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
segments.title: Staying on the bandstand at white dances, and playing Dixie
segments.summary: Rules of not mingling at white dances, how he felt, and insisting his band play Dixie.

segments.title: First dates, Emerette and Sundays at the Robin Hood
segments.summary: No dating before service; after discharge he went out with Emerette, Marino and Moran, hearing Paul Gayten and trying to sing.

segments.title: Meeting and marrying his wife
segments.summary: He met his wife at a club on Shrewsbury Road in 1948 and they married in 1949.

segments.title: Jitterbug, Lionel Hampton at the Municipal Auditorium and the first electric bass
segments.summary: He danced the jitterbug, and remembers Hampton's remark to the segregated balcony and the first electric bass in his band.

segments.title: Choosing Greenwald School of Music on the GI Bill
segments.summary: After considering the Navy and barber college he enrolled at Greenwald, taught by college faculty; alumni include Red Tyler and Earl Palmer.

segments.title: Courses and teachers at Greenwald
segments.summary: Nine-to-three days of history and music theory, arranging, piano and voice, with teachers Mr. Dean and Ms. Moulton.

segments.title: Notation, 32-bar form and piano method books
segments.summary: Learning notation, how he explains 32-bar form to young players, and the John Thompson piano books.

segments.title: Reel six
segments.summary: Reel number is sorted out and the date repeated.

segments.title: The old black Carnival downtown
segments.summary: He recalls the Carnival on Claiborne and the streets around it and wishes it had been filmed.

segments.title: Playing Carnival balls today and the slow season
segments.summary: He played eighteen balls last year, the season used to be longer, and he turns away low-paying club dates.

segments.title: Social clubs, Creole audiences and black audiences
segments.summary: Creole social-club crowds dance from the first note while other black crowds wait until half drunk.

segments.title: First white audiences: Jimmy Milano's, Jim Russell and the gondoliers
segments.summary: About 1956 he played a white club, was recommended to Natale's and moved from mostly black to mostly white audiences.

segments.title: Why white audiences accept him and black audiences make him work
segments.summary: Black audiences must warm up while whites accept him at once; he explains the mixed repertoire that gets him hired.

segments.title: Zulu ball, Irma Thomas and being asked back
segments.summary: Irma Thomas wishes blacks would hire her; the Zulus ask him to play their ball after being dissatisfied with others.

segments.title: Brass bands and playing on a parade truck in 1957
segments.summary: A band truck out of the Ninth Ward with Justin Adams on amplified guitar, white clubs he played for, and a brass band he cannot name.

segments.title: The roughest clubs and a riot at the Robin Hood
segments.summary: The San Jacinto and public halls had fights; a Sunday melee at the Robin Hood sent them over a fence.

segments.title: Robin Hood and Dew Drop nightlife, then and now
segments.summary: Clubs were full and safe in the 1940s; fear of crime has driven people to private clubs.

segments.title: The Autocrat Club and light-skinned black crowds
segments.summary: Dances at the Autocrat look white but are black New Orleanians, and a Covington dance is the same.

segments.title: Hiding money and equipment left in the car outside the Dew Drop
segments.summary: He never had to hide his pay and bands left equipment in cars at the Dew Drop.

segments.chapter: Race, pay and the color line
segments.title: Guarantees and percentages; hit-record popularity with white crowds
segments.summary: Flat pay with a contract split after hits; his popularity after 'When I Meet My Girl', girls mobbing him in Alexandria, and keeping business on the bandstand.

segments.chapter: Race, pay and the color line
segments.title: Black musicians and white women: the Cavaliers and Lee Allen
segments.summary: The Cavaliers' painter disguise and the story of driving Lee Allen to a white woman's house.

segments.chapter: Race, pay and the color line
segments.title: Why black men sought white women: forbidden fruit and status
segments.summary: He explains the attraction as forbidden fruit and social status, and says white men did it more.

segments.chapter: Race, pay and the color line
segments.title: Creole caste and the Autocrat back door
segments.summary: Blacks were once barred from the Autocrat; today it is led by a black president and he loves his Creole friends.

segments.chapter: Race, pay and the color line
segments.title: The Shreveport country club ramp and Sheck Snyder
segments.summary: Drummer Buddy Wade takes the bandstand ramp for a back door, and Sheck Snyder says he opposes interracial marriage.

segments.title: Playing for dancers, listeners and jazz festivals
segments.summary: He projects more for a seated audience and looks forward to playing the jazz festival.

segments.title: Songwriting and the new song Boogie Train
segments.summary: Dances do not inspire his songs; he writes professionally and describes a new record.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: The Blue Eagle, B.B. King, Sam Cooke and Jackie Wilson
segments.summary: A rough club run by the Mayor of Rampart Street; shows with B.B. King, Sam Cooke and Jackie Wilson, and the Dew Drop finale with Little Willie John and Ray Charles.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Whites at the Dew Drop and police harassment
segments.summary: Whites like Robert Mitchum came, but police kept most away.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Frank Painia's drinking and the Mobile gig split
segments.summary: Frank Painia booked an Alabama gig and took a cut; Ridgley recalls keeping beans in the pot.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: House band at the Dew Drop in 1956-58 and backing visiting stars
segments.summary: He played Friday to Sunday for two years, backing Faye Adams, Billy Wright and Little Richard.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Reviving the Dew Drop; Chris Kenner's key and fallen stars
segments.summary: Attendance rose when he arrived; wrong-key story with Chris Kenner, and stars who later came back down.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: The Dew Drop hotel and stranded artists
segments.summary: Frank's hotel housed James Brown, and Chuck Willis's saxophonist stayed behind.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Nose, the saxophonist Rufus Gore
segments.summary: How the sax player nicknamed Nose settled in New Orleans, was a nice man, and later repaired saxophones.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Rehearsing for new singers and simpler music
segments.summary: They learned singers' hits or got song lists; music was simpler, like Joe Turner finding his key.

segments.chapter: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
segments.title: Little Richard and offers to join road bands
segments.summary: Little Richard asked him on the road, as did Lloyd Price; Ridgley stayed independent.
